*Strongyloides stercoralis* has a unique free-living cycle, allowing it to persist in the environment.

qs.q: Which specific parasitic stage is typically excreted in human feces and detected during stool examinations for Strongyloides stercoralis?
qs.e: Unlike most nematodes, Strongyloides stercoralis excretes larvae rather than eggs in human feces. Filariform larvae represent the infective stage that penetrates the skin rather than the stage found in initial stool checks.

qs.q: What is the primary natural mode of human infection with Strongyloides stercoralis?
qs.e: Infection primarily occurs via skin penetration by filariform (L3) larvae, usually through barefoot contact with contaminated soil. Ingestion of contaminated food or water is a much less common route.

qs.q: What is the preferred pharmacological treatment for a patient diagnosed with uncomplicated Strongyloides stercoralis infection?
o: Albendazole as a single high dose
qs.e: Ivermectin at 200 µg/kg daily for 2 days is the preferred treatment, whereas albendazole is noted to be less effective. Longer courses of ivermectin are reserved for disseminated disease and hyperinfection.

qs.q: Which clinical feature is commonly observed during the pulmonary migration phase of Strongyloides stercoralis larvae?
qs.e: Larval migration through the lungs causes small alveolar hemorrhages, bronchopneumonia, and asthma-like symptoms, sometimes with larvae found in sputum. Urticarial tracks and perianal pruritus are cutaneous manifestations rather than pulmonary ones.

qs.q: What distinguishes the free-living cycle of Strongyloides stercoralis from its parasitic cycle?
o: Adult worms reproduce via unfertilized eggs
Infective larvae bypass the skin phase
qs.e: In the free-living cycle, rhabditiform larvae in feces develop into free-living adult males and females in the soil, which mate and produce eggs. The parasitic cycle involves direct human infection by filariform larvae penetrating the skin.

qs.q: During the migration phase of Strongyloides stercoralis larvae through the lungs, what pathological finding may occur in the alveoli and bronchioles?
qs.e: Pulmonary migration of larvae causes small hemorrhages in the alveoli and bronchioles. Caseous necrosis is characteristic of tuberculosis rather than nematode larval migration.

qs.q: Why can Strongyloides stercoralis cause lifelong infections in a patient even if they leave an endemic area and never encounter new soil?
qs.e: Autoinfection enables lifelong infection without the need for reinfection from external sources. Vector transmission is not a feature of threadworm biology.

qs.q: What is a well-known limitation of using ELISA serology to diagnose Strongyloides stercoralis infections?
o: High false-negative rate in immunocompetent hosts
qs.e: ELISA serology can suffer from cross-reactivity with other helminths. It generally possesses a high sensitivity around 95% rather than a high false-negative rate.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Strongyloides stercoralis is a soil-transmitted nematode that can persist for decades via autoinfection. It causes strongyloidiasis, ranging from asymptomatic infection to life‑threatening hyperinfection, especially in immunocompromised hosts.

sections.p: A tiny roundworm that lives in the small intestine. Unique ability to complete a free‑living cycle in soil and an internal autoinfection cycle, allowing chronic infection.
b: Endemic in tropical/subtropical regions and warm temperate zones
Transmission through skin contact with contaminated soil

sections.p: The smallest human‑infecting nematode (≈2 mm adult female). Females are parthenogenetic; males are rare. Larvae are rhabditiform (non‑infective) and filariform (infective).
b: Filariform larvae penetrate skin, migrate via bloodstream to lungs, then to gut

sections.p: Infective filariform larvae enter through bare skin, travel to lungs, ascend the trachea, are swallowed, and mature in the duodenum. Some larvae become rhabditiform, are excreted, or transform into filariform larvae within the host (autoinfection).
b: Direct skin contact with contaminated soil
Autoinfection can maintain infection for decades

sections.p: Strongyloidiasis presents as asymptomatic, chronic intestinal disease, or severe hyperinfection/disseminated disease. Hyperinfection occurs when immune control fails, leading to massive larval burden and bacterial sepsis.
b: Mild: intermittent abdominal pain, diarrhea, eosinophilia
Severe: respiratory distress, shock, Gram‑negative sepsis, meningitis

sections.p: Detect larvae in stool, duodenal aspirate, or serology. Sensitivity improves with multiple samples. In hyperinfection, larvae appear in sputum, BAL, or urine.
b: If microscopy unavailable, send stool for concentration technique to a reference lab.

t.b: Is the patient shedding larvae? Positive confirms infection; negative does not rule out low‑level disease.
Has the patient been exposed? Positive supports diagnosis, especially when stool is negative; cross‑reactivity possible.
Is there pulmonary involvement? Finding larvae indicates hyperinfection.

sections.p: Eradicate the parasite with ivermectin; alternative albendazole is less effective. Treat hyperinfection aggressively and manage secondary bacterial infections. Prevent reinfection by improving sanitation and wearing footwear.
b: Ivermectin: kills all larval stages, preferred for safety and efficacy
Albendazole: second line, lower cure rates
Supportive care: oxygen, fluids, antibiotics for sepsis

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams.
b: Hyperinfection risk ↑ with steroids, HTLV‑1, HIV, chemotherapy.
Eosinophilia may be absent in severe disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Shock, unexplained fever, or meningitis in a known case

faq.q: Why can Strongyloides infection last a lifetime?
faq.a: Because larvae can reinfect the host internally without leaving the body.

faq.q: What drugs increase the risk of hyperinfection?
faq.a: Corticosteroids, other immunosuppressants, and HTLV‑1 infection.
It is common in chronic infection but may be normal in hyperinfection.
